## Overview

The UK Government’s Green Book sets out how to appraise costs, benefits and risks to achieve public sector objectives. It recommends the Five Case Model as the standard framework for developing robust business cases for projects and programmes. APMG International’s Better Business Cases qualification is based on the ‘Five Case Model’ methodology – a best-practice approach originally developed for the public sector to guide strategic planning and investment decisions at the government level.

Better Business Cases certification helps professionals build strong, value-driven proposals that win support and funding.

The digital content will take approximately 18 hours to complete (although some learners may wish to spend longer to help prepare more effectively) and there is additional UK Government Guidance to support your study. Note: there is no exam voucher included in this product. If you do wish to purchase this course with the exam you can do so here. Alternatively, you may purchase the exam at a later date. However, if you do so we recommend not leaving it too long after completing the course and you ideally sit the exam within a 4-week period to maintain focus and ensure suitable knowledge is retained.

## Prerequisites

There are no formal pre-requisites for Better Business Cases Foundation.

### Target Audience

Better Business Cases certification is aimed at professionals who play a key role in creating, delivering, or reporting the value of investments, and is suitable for anyone who:

- Wants to deepen their understanding of Better Business Cases processes and techniques.
- Is responsible for the successful delivery of programmes and projects, such as Senior Responsible Owners (SROs) or Programme Directors.
- Is responsible for developing a business case for investment, such as Project Managers, Project Team members and other specialist advisors.
- Is involved in the scrutiny and review of investment proposals.

## Outline

Throughout this course, you will learn to work effectively with a team to develop a strong business case. The content is covered in detail within the following lessons.

Introduction to Better Business Cases

This lesson will cover the purpose, value and benefits of Better Business Cases and explain why robust business cases are fundamental to successful programmes and projects. Learners will understand the causes of project failure, the role of business cases in supporting decision-making, and the relationship between projects, programmes and organisational strategy.

Programmes, Projects and the Business Case

This lesson will cover the characteristics of programmes and projects, their relationship to organisational strategy, and the governance arrangements that support successful investment decisions. Learners will understand programme and project assurance, business case ownership, and how Better Business Cases aligns with recognised project and programme management methodologies.

Overview of the Five Case Model

This lesson will cover the principles of the Five Case Model and its role within business case development. Learners will understand the purpose of the Strategic, Economic, Commercial, Financial and Management Cases and how each contributes to robust investment decision-making.

Business Case Development Process and Types of Business Case

This lesson will cover the stages of business case development and the different business case products used throughout the investment lifecycle. Learners will understand the purpose of the Strategic Outline Case, Outline Business Case, Full Business Case and Business Justification Case, alongside the ten-step business case development process.

Determining the Strategic Context

This lesson will cover the activities required to establish strategic fit and confirm the organisational context for an investment proposal. Learners will understand strategic assessment, organisational objectives, governance considerations and the relationship between programmes, projects and strategic portfolios.

Scoping the Proposal – The Strategic Case and Preferred Way Forward

This lesson will cover how to establish the case for change and identify a preferred way forward. Learners will understand spending objectives, business needs, scope, benefits, risks, constraints, dependencies, critical success factors, and the process used to identify and evaluate long-list options.

Planning the Scheme – Determining Value for Money

This lesson will cover how value for money is assessed through appraisal of short-listed options. Learners will understand economic appraisal, costs and benefits, optimism bias, benefits appraisal, risk appraisal, sensitivity analysis and the selection of a preferred option.

Planning the Scheme – Commercial and Financial Cases

This lesson will cover the commercial and financial considerations associated with investment proposals. Learners will understand procurement strategies, risk apportionment, payment mechanisms, affordability, funding requirements and the financial assessments required to support business case approval.

Planning for Successful Delivery – The Management Case

This lesson will cover the arrangements required to support successful project and programme delivery. Learners will understand project management, change management, benefits realisation, risk management, assurance and post-project evaluation arrangements used within the Management Case.

Procuring the Proposal, Reviewing the Business Case and Exam Preparation

This lesson will cover the final stages of the business case lifecycle, including procurement activities, contract arrangements and business case review. Learners will consolidate their understanding of the Five Case Model, business case development process and Foundation examination requirements through revision and exam-focused activities.

### Exams and Assessments

Please not that this eLearning course option does not include the Better Business Cases Foundation exam. If you do wish to purchase this course with the exam you can do so here. Should learners wish to progress and purchase / take the Foundation exam it consists of:

- 50 multiple-choice questions.
- 40 minutes to complete the exam.
- 25 marks are required to pass (25/50) — 50%.

This is a closed-book exam.

Full details of how to take an online APMG exam can be found on its website: Help & Support | APMG International

### What’s Included

- 12 months access to self-paced digital content (estimated 18 hours)
- Sample examination paper

You will be directed to download personal copies of the UK Government’s ‘Guide to Developing the Programme Business Case’ and the ‘Guide to Developing the Project Business Case’.

This content has been developed by QA with the use of APMG International’s Better Business Cases Certification with permission of the APM Group Ltd.

## Learning outcomes

Key things that you will learn on this course include:

- The philosophy and underlying rationale of the Five Case Model methodology.
- The different types of business case, their purpose, who is responsible for them, and when they are required in the development of a spending proposal.
- The development of the business case in relation to other recognized and recommended best practice for programme and project management.

# Autonomous vessel facility to power future maritime skills

24 November 2026

Southampton Solent University is set to expand its globally renowned maritime teaching and learning portfolio with a new facility dedicated to maritime autonomy, helping to develop the next generation of talent in one of the sector's fastest-growing areas.

Following a successful bid for capital funding from the Office for Students, Solent will launch an ambitious project to establish a dedicated Uncrewed Surface Vessel (USV) learning facility in Southampton.

The facility will provide students with first-hand experience of the technologies transforming the maritime industry, including autonomous vessels, advanced sonar systems, robotics and high-performance computing. Designed to support the growing use of USVs in areas such as hydrographic surveying, environmental monitoring and port security, the project will equip graduates with the practical skills increasingly sought by employers across the maritime sector.

Integrated across a range of existing courses in maritime, engineering and computing disciplines, the new facility will create a unique multidisciplinary learning environment where students can design, programme, operate and maintain autonomous systems. They will also gain experience of managing complex autonomous operations, including how multiple vessels can interact safely and effectively to complete a range of tasks.

The investment reflects the increasing importance of maritime autonomy both regionally and nationally, with industry demand continuing to grow for professionals who can develop, manage and operate autonomous technologies.

Jonathan Ridley, Associate Pro Vice-Chancellor at Southampton Solent University, said:

"USV technology is advancing rapidly, creating exciting opportunities across the maritime sector. There is a clear demand across the region for people with the right skills and knowledge to support this growth.

"This project will ensure our graduates from a range of subject areas can apply their specialist expertise in the context of maritime autonomy and are well prepared for the careers of the future."

The new facility will build on Solent's extensive maritime infrastructure, which already includes the University's 60-metre towing tank, Maritime Simulation Centre, specialist maritime laboratories and Ship Handling Centre at Timsbury Lake.

By combining these established facilities with new autonomous technologies, Solent is further strengthening its position as a leading provider of maritime education, training and applied research. Graduates will leave with the career-ready expertise needed to help drive the future of autonomous maritime technology and support the UK's ambition to remain a global leader in maritime innovation.

The new USV learning facility complements the University's wider investment in maritime innovation through the Solent Maritime Autonomy, Research and Training (SMART) Centre, which opened in January 2026.

Based at Solent's East Park Terrace campus, the SMART Centre brings together education, research and industry engagement to accelerate the development and adoption of maritime autonomous technologies. The centre provides a collaborative environment where students, researchers and industry partners can work together on real-world challenges, helping to advance innovation in autonomous vessels, robotics, artificial intelligence and marine data systems.

Through specialist facilities, applied research projects and close collaboration with industry, the SMART Centre supports regional and national priorities for maritime growth while helping to ensure the UK remains at the forefront of autonomous maritime capability. The centre also creates new opportunities for students to gain industry-relevant experience and develop the advanced technical skills needed to succeed in a rapidly evolving maritime sector.

title: Russia “ever-present danger” after Litvinenko murder warns KC | ULaw
text:
24 Nov 2026

Ben Emmerson KC, a leading human rights barrister who acted for the Litvinenko family, brands Vladimir Putin a “common criminal dressed up as a head of state”.

He describes Russian state-sponsored assassinations as a form of “asymmetrical warfare” against the West designed to de-stabilise their institutions.

On the continuing threat from Russia: “It’s an ever-present danger in every respect.”

On Putin, he says - recalling his opening speech at the public inquiry into Litvinenko’s death: “Putin is no more than a common criminal dressed up as a head of state.”

On Russian state-sponsored assassinations: “It’s a form of asymmetrical warfare designed to destabilise the state and its institutions.”

### NEW PODCAST SERIES: Inside the Case

Eighth episode: "The Poisoning of Alexander Litvinenko"

Alexander Litvinenko died on November 23, 2006, in London, aged 43, after being poisoned with radioactive polonium-210.

Twenty years on, the barrister who represented his widow warns that Russia remains an “ever-present danger” to the West.

Ben Emmerson KC, who achieved the setting up of the public inquiry into Litvinenko’s murder, repeats his denunciation at that inquiry of Vladimir Putin as “no more than a common criminal dressed up as a head of state”.

He warns that Russian state-sponsored assassinations form part of a wider strategy to destabilise Western nations and undermine their institutions.

His comments come in the latest episode of The University of Law’s video podcast, Inside the Case, where he also criticises the West for its inconsistent stance towards Putin and warns of the dangers of undermining international law.

His warnings come ahead of the 20th anniversary of Litvinenko’s death on November 23 and coincides with the publication of his widow Marina’s new memoir, A Life in Fragments: Our Love, His Murder, My Resistance, published by Bloomsbury on 5 November 2026.

In it she talks of her struggle to secure justice and her aim for her husband’s murder to be seen as part of a wider pattern of attacks of opponents, extending beyond Russia’s borders.

The 2016 public inquiry in London concluded that her husband was murdered by Andrei Lugovoy and Dmitry Kovtun, probably acting under the direction of the FSB - and that Putin probably approved the operation.

In 2021 the European Court of Human Rights held Russia responsible for Litvinenko’s death and ordered it to pay Marina 100,000 Euros in damages - which has never been paid. The men identified as responsible have not faced any criminal trial. One has since died.

Emmerson describes the battle Marina Litvenenko faced in securing a public inquiry - where she was at risk of legal costs that would mean she would lose her home.

Theresa May, then Prime Minister, had refused the public inquiry. “She [Marina] was treated like a nuisance litigant at this point, and the government not only refused to conduct the inquiry, but they refused to agree a costs arrangement that would enable her to go into this without fear of having to pay a huge government bill.”

The risk of costs “was being held against her over her head like a Sword of Damocles” and “being done deliberately to discourage her from going on with it.”

But, he says, she was determined to go ahead. “Marina is an extraordinary woman. She was determined, obviously, but dignified and courageous every step of the way.

“She told me at one point she couldn’t really move on with her life until she had, if you like, done justice to the man whom she loved, the love of her life, namely to pursue that question…. on whose orders was he killed? The very question that he himself had posed in his dying days.”

The decision to assassinate Litvinenko, Emmerson says, was taken at the “very top of the state of the Russian Federation - and “fundamentally, it was a murder - albeit it was deeply embedded in international politics - it was “a murder of a man for his beliefs.”

There was evidence, he adds, of Putin’s close relationship with one of the murderers: when evidence of his guilt became conclusive, Putin “called him in and pinned a medal for services to the motherland onto his chest.”

On the opening day of the inquiry, when Emmerson had made his speech about Putin being a criminal dressed up as a head of state, within hours Russian fighter jets buzzed the coast of Cornwall, entering British airspace and then leaving.

It was an unprecedented case, he recalls. “It was a carefully planned operation which had involved two or three visits to London. And once the isotope had been identified, it was possible for the police to trace the movements of these two individuals as though they were Hansel and Gretel leaving a trail behind them.”

In the end, the proof turned on a collection of debris in the u-bend of a wash basin in a hotel bedroom because security cameras could prove there was only one person inside that room at that time. After the poisoning, the excess polonium had been poured down the sink and collected among the debris in the u-bend.

“It’s often said that there’s one piece of evidence in a case that really everything turns on. It can often be something very apparently insignificant. And in a way, the dirt and the filth that went into this murder found its expression in the fact that the final key to proving their guilt was the dirty debris in the u-bend of a public [wash basin].”

The case was a “life-changing experience for me”, he says, “where the stakes were as high as they could possibly be, with the client who earned my admiration and respect within the first meeting that we had. She’s the epitome of a person with dignity and courage.”

# A run to remember

Running in memory of our dear friend Darren Hodgson.

Passionate trail runner, outdoor enthusiast and seeker of all things adventurous, our dearly missed colleague and friend made it his mission to persuade his team to tackle the “Dirty Double.” What he was unable to do, his team mates finished for him.

Three years ago, our dearly departed and much-missed MD, Darren Hodgson, a passionate trail runner, outdoor enthusiast and seeker of all things adventurous, invited a group of colleagues to join him for a Lakeland Trails run in Hawkshead. Despite, or perhaps because of, the atrocious weather that weekend, countless memories were made. Daz soon made it his mission to persuade the team to tackle the “Dirty Double” with him, a long-held ambition involving a trail run around Helvellyn on the Saturday followed by Ullswater on the Sunday. Sadly, it was an ambition that would ultimately go unfulfilled.

When news of his passing broke, thoughts quickly turned to how best to honour a man who meant so much to so many. His Lakeland Trails teammates soon signed up to complete the Dirty Double under the team name Hodgson’s Trail Runners, with Pete Hanslip from London joining Adam, Dan, Rick and Paul from the North West tutor team.

The races took place on 31 October and 1 November, just a week after Storm Babet and at a time of year when conditions in the Lakes are usually, at best, challenging. It therefore felt almost spiritual that throughout the entire weekend the sun shone over the fells, the skies remained clear and there was barely a breath of wind. It genuinely felt as though Daz was there in spirit, looking after his lads and blessing them with weather more akin to early summer than late autumn.

Having benefited from Daz’s extensive trail running experience and encyclopaedic knowledge of the courses at Hawkshead in April 2024, the group quickly realised just how much they had relied on his guidance. The Helvellyn and Ullswater routes proved far more technical, with steep climbs, difficult descents and demanding terrain offering little opportunity to relax and admire the stunning scenery.

The weekend nearly got off to a disastrous start, something that certainly wouldn’t have happened on Daz’s watch. An unnamed member of the team briefly misplaced Rick’s car keys during a 20-metre walk back to the car, prompting five grown men to frantically search through grass verges and under parked vehicles in a mild state of panic. One can only imagine Daz looking down and thoroughly enjoying the spectacle.

The challenging Helvellyn course was largely navigated without incident. Pete Hanslip surged to the front early on, despite relatively limited trail-running experience, and spent much of the race challenging the leading pack. Unfortunately, on the descent from Helvellyn, Paul suffered a fall and dislocated his shoulder. After bravely hobbling across the finish line and making a brief appearance in the medical tent, he opted to delay a trip to A&E in favour of joining the team for the traditional post-race debrief at the pub. Meanwhile, Rick, Dan and Adam all completed the course with impressive times on what was a demanding and relentlessly hilly route.

The following morning, Pete, Rick, Dan and Adam boarded a boat bound for the start line of the second instalment of the Dirty Double, no small achievement given the aching legs and weary bodies from the previous day’s efforts. During the picturesque 30-minute crossing, a guitarist entertained passengers on board. One particularly poignant moment came when, at Rick’s request, he performed The Gambler in tribute to Daz.

The four teammates once again successfully negotiated a technically challenging course on tired legs. Pete again found himself near the front of the field, followed by Rick, Dan and finally Adam. Adam’s finish provided a fitting callback to Hawkshead 2024, when he crossed the line clutching a hamburger, a moment that Daz often laughed about. This time, he crossed carrying a slice of Pete Hanslip’s ham and pineapple pizza, perhaps not the most natural choice for Adam’s palate, as anyone who knows him will appreciate.

With the running complete, the team returned to their accommodation before heading to the local watering hole, the Brotherswater Inn. Once again, it felt as though Daz was looking after his team. The unassuming country pub somehow produced what many agreed was one of the finest Sunday roasts and sticky toffee puddings they had ever experienced. Although, to be fair, 30 kilometres of running and a few Lakeland beers may also have played their part.

Daz took immense pride in organising the Hawkshead trail runs and in seeing colleagues encourage one another to get fitter, healthier and more involved in trail running. The Dirty Double weekend, and the trail-running team that continues to take part, are just some of the many examples of the legacy he left behind. A legacy that continues to inspire those who knew him and will live on for many years to come.

# New Funding Rules for Level 7 Accountancy Professional Apprenticeships Explained

From 18 December 2026, the Level 7 Accountancy Professional Apprenticeship will include a mandatory ICAEW or ACCA professional qualification as part of the apprenticeship.

Equivalent to a Master’s degree, the Level 7 apprenticeship offers a programme which will develop business leaders of the future. The programme aligns with globally recognised professional accountancy qualifications, as well as providing structured support and guidance for each apprentice’s wider development.

From 18 December 2026, the Level 7 Accountancy Professional Apprenticeship will include a mandatory ICAEW or ACCA professional qualification as part of the apprenticeship.

So, what does this mean for employers?

1. Qualification costs can be funded through the apprenticeship

Eligible costs can now be covered through apprenticeship funding, including:

- Tuition and training

- Registration fees

- Examination fees

- One resit per mandatory exam

This can significantly reduce the additional costs traditionally associated with professional accountancy qualifications.

2. One integrated programme

The qualification is mandated, apprentices will achieve the apprenticeship by successfully completing the required exams, with no separate End-Point Assessment (EPA).

3. Increased funding

The funding band for the new Level 7 Accountancy Professional Apprenticeship will increase from £21,000 to £26,000 to cover tuition, exam and registration costs.

Level 7 eligibility

Government-funded Level 7 apprenticeships are restricted to apprentices aged 16-21, or 22-24 where they have an EHCP or are, or have been, in local authority care.

What does this mean for your organisation?

By embedding professional qualifications within the apprenticeship, employers can benefit from greater funding support and a clearer pathway to developing professionally qualified accountants.

For example, if you are a non-levy employer looking to enrol an ICAEW Level 7 apprentice, you would benefit from the following:

- 100% fully funded apprenticeship which now includes student registration fees and exam fees

- Class 1 employer National Insurance savings

We are excited about the opportunities these changes create and would be happy to discuss what they mean for your current or future Level 7 apprentices. To find out more please contact us.

# What the Milburn review could mean for employers hiring young people

The Milburn review proposes changes to apprenticeship funding, recruitment and support for young people entering work. We explore what the recommendations could mean for employers and how businesses can widen access to opportunities while developing the skills trainees need as AI changes their roles.

According to the Milburn review, nearly one million 16- to 24-year-olds are out of education, employment or training, whilst six in ten of them have never had a job. The final Milburn review asks what it would take to give more young people that first opportunity and help them build a career from it.

For employers, the recommendations raise three questions:

- Could it become easier to create a trainee role?
- How can recruitment reach young people who have had fewer chances to gain experience?
- What should a first job teach someone when AI is changing the work junior staff do?

The review is independent, and its recommendations would require government decisions before taking effect, however, employers can already act on several of the issues it raises. Read the final Milburn review

## Could it become easier to hire an apprentice?

Milburn’s recommendations could make apprenticeships easier for employers to access by improving funding, simplifying administration and providing more help to find and support young recruits.

He proposes fully funding under-25 apprenticeships from levy receipts, regardless of employer size, with no specific recruitment limits. The existing £2,000 hiring payment for eligible non-levy employers would rise to £2,500 and extend to levy payers. This could help a small practice or finance team meet the costs of supervising a new trainee and give larger employers an additional reason to expand their intake. GOV.UK

The review also recommends replacing employer levy balances and levy transfers over time with direct funding linked to employer demand and government priorities. For employers, this could reduce the administration involved in arranging funding and make it easier to plan recruitment around their skills needs. The eventual funding rules would determine how much flexibility employers gain.

Finding suitable candidates could become more straightforward too. A proposed Youth Opportunity Service would give employers a named adviser to coordinate recruitment and support, while a national account service would help businesses recruiting across several locations. Employers could benefit from a clearer point of contact when they need help with a new recruit, particularly if they have limited HR capacity.

Milburn also proposes allocating an initial 10% of the apprenticeship budget to strategic authorities for employer engagement and local opportunities. Better connections between employers, providers and local careers services could help a firm reach candidates who would otherwise never consider accountancy.

For First Intuition, these proposals could help employers create more Level 3 and Level 4 roles and support trainees towards professional qualification. A simpler funding route would be particularly valuable if it gives employers confidence to commit to an intake and plan its development over several years.

However, there are questions about who would benefit. Milburn proposes reducing government apprenticeship funding for people aged 25 and over by 25%, which could increase employers’ costs when developing existing staff or recruiting career changers. He also supports expanding higher apprenticeships, although the review leaves Level 7 eligibility unresolved. First Intuition would like eligibility extended through age 24 so that more young trainees can continue towards professional qualification.

These recommendations give employers a prospect of more accessible funding and coordinated support. Their practical value will depend on the government’s response and whether the resulting system makes it easier to recruit, train and retain an apprentice.

## How can recruitment reach young people who have had fewer chances to gain experience?

The review’s employer-led ‘First Chance’ initiative calls for more entry-level jobs, apprenticeships and meaningful work experience, alongside accessible recruitment that recognises potential and removes unnecessary experience requirements. Read the recommendations

Employers can reach young people with fewer opportunities by advertising placements through local schools, colleges and community organisations, and working with organisations such as Access Accountancy. Clear vacancy descriptions should explain the work, pay, entry requirements, training and progression, including which skills applicants will develop on the job.

Selection should give candidates different ways to demonstrate their potential. School projects, caring responsibilities, volunteering and part-time work can provide examples of teamwork and responsibility. A short task, such as reviewing simple figures and explaining what needs checking, can reveal curiosity and judgement. Sharing the interview format and explaining how to request adjustments can also help candidates prepare.

Make work experience purposeful, with clear tasks, a named colleague for support and an introduction to everyday workplace expectations. Providing equipment and help with travel or meal costs where possible can make participation easier.

Finish with specific feedback and practical next steps, helping students explain their experience in future applications. A well-supported placement can help someone make an informed career choice and introduce an employer to a future apprentice.

We have more advice on how best to engage with school and college leavers here.

## What should a first job teach someone when AI is changing the work junior staff do?

The Milburn review proposes making AI skills training available to every young person and creating an ‘AI Youth Observatory’ to track changes in entry-level jobs and tasks. For employers, this raises the question, as technology takes on tasks that trainees previously learnt through doing, how will new starters build the knowledge and judgement they need to progress? Read the review’s recommendations

A first job should help someone understand how their work contributes to the organisation, what reliable information looks like and when to question a result. In accountancy, technical knowledge provides the foundation for checking whether an answer makes sense. Employers can build this understanding by asking trainees to explain their reasoning, investigate discrepancies and discuss the consequences of an error.

Alongside First Intuition’s accountancy training, Decoded’s expertise in data and AI can help employers develop these learning opportunities. A trainee could check an AI-generated summary against source figures, investigate an unexpected result and explain whether it changes the conclusion. They would practise using technology while learning about data quality, the limits of its output and when to seek advice.

The ability to communicate that finding matters too. SkillsLab helps learners practise asking questions, explaining information, collaborating and responding to feedback. Line managers can reinforce this by demonstrating a task, giving the trainee an opportunity to try it and discussing what they could improve. Regular conversations also help new starters become comfortable admitting uncertainty and asking for support.

Together, these experiences develop the multi-dimensional professional who can combine technical expertise, digital capability and human skills. Employers can start by reviewing the tasks in a junior role, identifying what each one teaches and planning how trainees will continue to develop those skills as technology changes the work.

## What employers can do before their next intake

At Continua Learning Group, we bring together First Intuition’s accountancy training, SkillsLab’s professional skills development and Decoded’s expertise in data, digital and AI. For employers planning their next intake, those perspectives come together in three decisions.

- Open up the route in. Review where you advertise placements and vacancies, and remove experience requirements you can replace with a fair assessment of potential.
- Plan the first few months. Give trainees meaningful work, a named person for support and regular feedback. Identify one task that technology has changed and decide how trainees will learn the underlying skills.
- Show where the role can lead. Set out which qualifications and responsibilities a trainee could progress to, and discuss how you would support that progression before they reach the next stage.

The government’s response will determine which funding and support proposals go ahead. Employers can use their next intake to widen access to a first job and give new starters a clearer path from their first assignment to the next stage of their career.

## 40 Linklaters colleagues in London will learn to build and deploy their own AI agents and workflows through Multiverse's AI training

Global law firm Linklaters is partnering with Multiverse, the upskilling platform for AI and tech adoption, to develop the AI skills of its London-based teams.

Learners will predominantly come from the firm's Business Teams, the centralised specialist departments that play a crucial role in supporting Linklaters' lawyers. They will enrol in Multiverse's AI apprenticeships, which will equip them with the skills to become AI-fluent practitioners who design, build and roll out AI solutions.

Linklaters is piloting the partnership as part of its strategy to drive AI adoption across the firm, supporting it to deliver better outcomes for clients, work more efficiently, and strengthen how it competes as legal services evolve.

Victoria Matthews, Head of HR, LAI and Applied Intelligence, Linklaters, said: “AI is changing how we work at pace, and we want our people to feel ready for that change. By investing in AI skills, we're helping colleagues stay ahead of new technology, develop workflows that make a difference to their teams every day, build capabilities that support their future careers, and showing current and future talent that Linklaters will invest in their development.”

Sarah Barnard, Director of AI Delivery and Co-Founder, Applied Intelligence, Linklaters, said: “Our approach to AI is about much more than deploying new tools. It's about how we operate as a firm and equipping our people with the skills to use AI effectively. Investing in and enhancing those capabilities across our Business Teams will help us work smarter, collaborate differently and ultimately deliver even greater value for our clients.”

Multiverse's latest skills intelligence data, based on assessments of 14,508 UK employees, found that legal services workers spend around two hours a day on data tasks that could be automated, and 27.8% of that time is spent ineffectively. As a result, the sector loses an estimated 16 working days per person each year.

To close this gap, Linklaters has already been investing in AI at pace. Last year it unveiled a team of dedicated AI Lawyers, a group of AI experts that advise teams on how to integrate AI into their work. This industry first strategy has been working to encourage peer-to-peer adoption of the technology across Linklaters' global offices and practice groups.

Working with Multiverse will extend that peer-to-peer capability. The partnership will give colleagues the skills to build AI into their own work, on top of the AI tools already available across the firm, so that they have the knowledge to improve their workflows and upskill their teams.

Euan Blair, Founder and CEO of Multiverse, said: “Linklaters is showing what it looks like to put AI to work in one of the world's most demanding professional environments. By giving people at every level the skills to build their own agents and workflows, they are turning AI from something people hear about into something people use every day. We're proud to partner with them.”

Through Multiverse's on-the-job learning model, each Linklaters learner will apply what they learn to real projects, with the aim of improving the speed and quality of delivery to colleagues and clients and freeing up time for deeper, more strategic work.

The AI-Powered Productivity programme will teach colleagues to use available AI tools confidently in their everyday work, while AI Solutions Builder, delivered on the Level 4 AI and Automation Practitioner standard, will teach them to design, build and deploy AI agents and automated workflows.

Learners will work with expert Multiverse coaches and learn alongside peers, then apply each new skill to a project in their own team, such as automating a recurring process or building an agent that speeds up an internal request. Multiverse tracks each learner's progress and the impact of their projects, so Linklaters can see the value that the training has delivered.

Behind Mastry sits an AI engineering team across Edinburgh and London, which Col Mackenzie, VP, AI Engineering, leads. We sat down with Col and asked him how his team came together, who they are and what makes them different.

In short: Multiverse's Edinburgh AI Hub began with one phone call. The team runs without hierarchy and hires for talent wherever it hides. Its leader worked as a professional magician for years, and its people include a member of the band Anchor Lane and an engineer who joined straight from a chip shop.

Let's dig into it.

## As the leader of our AI engineering team at Multiverse, what does your role involve?

My job is to build every part of our AI engineering capability: the platforms we create, the software development lifecycle we follow and the culture that makes a team perform at a high level. I also lead our Edinburgh AI hub, and I want it to be the most appealing place to work in tech in Scotland.

There's one key idea behind my approach to leadership: to improve my own work, I need to be around people who are better than me. I know that I can learn something from everybody, whatever their background or seniority. I've had a varied career, and living and working alongside very different people proved that to me.

## Why did Multiverse build an AI engineering hub in Edinburgh?

Jay Richman, Multiverse's Chief Product & Technology Officer, called me to ask if I'd consider a new role heading up the AI Engineering team. It was my first week of paternity leave in my previous role, and I wasn't looking to change jobs. But the problem Multiverse is tackling appealed to me. If we do our job right, we're building a product that will have a generational impact on the economy and society, making sure that technology works for people, not against them.

Then Jay mentioned three days a week in London. I have a family and I wasn't planning to move away from Scotland, so I made him an offer: open an office in Edinburgh and I'll run it. He came back the next day and agreed.

Scotland has a large, untapped talent pool, with strong AI-focused universities and a lot of research. More people are moving north for a different pace of life. I also had a good contact book of engineers, so we bootstrapped the hub quickly. Word spread from there.

The Edinburgh engineering team doesn't do anything different from the London team. We are one engineering team, working towards a common goal.

## How do you build a team where everyone can contribute, whatever their seniority?

For me, there is no hierarchy, and that is hard to build. Someone told me recently that they weren't sure they could come to me directly. They thought they had to go to their boss first. I said, why would you? It doesn't matter if you're a junior engineer in a different part of the business. Come and talk to me.

Everybody makes a unique contribution, and the hidden gems often sit in unexpected places. That has held true throughout my career. It carries over neatly into software, because there are so many perspectives on how you build a product.

## What did a career as a magician teach you about leading a team?

I still call myself a magician! I worked at it professionally for a long time: magic, hypnosis and pickpocketing (though I always gave everything back!). It taught me more than any other role I've had. I learned how to deal with stakeholders, how to deal with all kinds of people and how to manage under pressure. There were so many transferable skills.

## Who is on the team, and what might surprise people?

Most of the Edinburgh office plays an instrument: bass guitar, drums, piano. Nobody sings, so if you can, you're welcome to take the stage…

One of our AI managers is in a band that's played Download Festival, one writes orchestral music; another used to play in a hard rock band.

Another member of the team can build almost anything. Years ago, before having access to AI, he wanted a 3D printer and couldn't buy one. So he researched the components, ordered a pile of electrical parts and built one from scratch. That's famously difficult to do.

## Why does Multiverse hire junior AI engineers?

We're an upskilling company, so we should invest in the next generation. When I joined, the industry trend was not to hire juniors. I wanted the opposite. I was a mechanic once, and I learned from a proper journeyman (a skilled tradesperson in the field). I wanted to test that model in tech: pair a junior engineer with a high-performing senior and see if we can incubate their skills.

Then I got a message on LinkedIn from someone who was finishing his degree, asking if I had a job. I get a million messages like that, but his was good, so we spoke. He went through our full hiring process and smashed it. His only previous job was in a chip shop. Now he works in one of the best AI roles in the country, and he's exceptional.

## How do those backgrounds show up in the work?

They think around corners. Give anyone on the team a problem and they find a creative route to it. That's what I like about solving problems in the office. If we stand at a whiteboard, there isn't a problem we can't solve, because someone has usually sketched out a whole solution and said, let's just try that. The ability to pull a solution apart and put it back together is very strong. It's fun, too.

## Will AI replace people, and how does that shape the way you build Mastry?

Humans can be augmented with AI, as they have been with other technology. The industrial revolution let us manufacture faster. Well, AI lets us do knowledge work faster. You effectively have an expert you can ask anything, at any time, and you can hand tasks to it. But it still needs a huge amount of human context and judgement to get the best from it.

I think AI replacing people is unlikely, but AI replacing some work is certain. The transition will be the difficult thing to get right: people need to understand how their work changes when they can use AI to remove repetitive manual toil. That frees them for higher-level tasks and strategic thinking. What you do with the time back is up to you.

# Moving your team from AI awareness to everyday habits

Share:

Most teams no longer wonder what AI is. If you ask people at work to define an LLM or name some tools, many can do it easily. If you ask how often they use AI in their daily work, the answers are less certain. People know about AI across the board, but usage isn’t as consistent as awareness. This creates continuity issues, exacerbated by shadow AI, as people turn to unapproved tools outside IT’s view. If people use different levels of AI integration and different AIs, it can create a logjam.

This is the main challenge for most AI productivity training today. Just knowing about digital tools isn’t enough for teams to see real value. We need to look at how managers can help employees move from passive tech users to active productivity champions. This can turn routine admin tasks into time-saving wins, freeing up time for more strategic, creative work.

## Where AI awareness faces friction

Corndel’s research on workplace AI use supports this. About 97% of HR leaders say their business offers AI training. Only 39% of employees say they have received it, with just 14% thinking the training is very effective. The real problem is what happens between the classroom and the desk.

Training days help people understand new ideas, but that grasp often fades when work gets busy. People return to old habits because they feel easier and safer under pressure. Teams might learn digital skills once, then forget them when deadlines hit. Real change needs practice on the job, not only a one-time session that ends when the laptop closes.

### From passive user to productivity champion

A passive AI user waits for someone else to suggest how to use it, then forgets about it by the next week. An active productivity champion notices problems in their own work and uses AI on their own. This difference may seem small, but it separates teams that only talk about AI from those that use it every day.

Building this habit takes more than a single workshop or a list of prompts. People need to see AI solve a real problem in their own job, not just a general example from a presentation. When someone saves real time on their own task, it becomes much easier to do it again next time.

### Turn routine admin into regular AI reps

Personal productivity and digital skills are built through the small, repeatable tasks that fill most workdays. Meeting notes, first-draft emails or data entry en massé no longer need to start from scratch. These tasks should become a daily AI practice.

If you can get your team to choose one regular task each week and have an AI tool draft it before they start, you'll save time. A weekly report can become a five-minute edit instead of a 40-minute write. Meeting notes can turn into a clear summary in seconds, ready for a quick review.

Small, low-risk tasks are the best place to start because the risk is low while people build the habit. No one needs approval to draft an internal email in a new way. This makes admin work a great place to build daily AI habits, without needing a formal course.

## How managers can build the habit loop

Habits form through repetition, so managers need to make it easy for people to repeat new behaviours. One simple method is to spot a task that AI handled well, write down the steps that worked, then share that process with the whole team.

Weekly team check-ins are a good time for this. Give someone a chance to share the AI shortcut they used that week, even if it’s small. Over time, this habit spreads through the team and sharing becomes part of the culture instead of just another task.

Managers who show the behaviour themselves usually see it catch on faster. If a manager uses AI to draft an agenda or summarise a document, others notice and follow. People are more likely to copy what leaders do than what they say in a training session.

### What frees up when AI takes the admin

The goal of building these habits isn’t just to work faster, but to use the time you save better. Corndel’s research shows that making more time is only the first step. Leaders need to decide how to use that extra time wisely.

The hours saved on admin should go toward work that only people can do well. There will always be tasks you wouldn’t trust an AI to do. Anything client- or customer-facing should still be handled by a person, with any work an LLM produces checked rigorously. If you don’t plan for this, extra admin will fill the time. If the purpose is time-saving, we probably don’t need to tell you what the issue is here.

## Building AI productivity training that actually sticks

Awareness efforts and one-time sessions are useful, but they can’t create lasting change on their own. Real AI productivity training combines practical digital skills with ongoing coaching to turn good habits into teamwide practices.

Corndel’s Working Smarter with AI apprenticeship helps people use AI for real productivity gains in their own jobs. For more advanced teams, the Automation with AI programme teaches how to turn manual workflows into automated ones. Both are part of the Corndel AI Academy, run with Imperial College Business School and Microsoft.

Ready to build lasting AI habits across your team?

Turning AI awareness into real habits comes from small, repeated successes that managers spread across their teams. You need to lead by example. Begin with the admin tasks people already dislike; the habit will grow from there.

# Why AI won't take accountants jobs

Kaplan · 7 minute read · Published 25 Nov, 2026

## Table of contents

Share article

There’s no denying that AI is changing the way accountants work. Tasks that once took hours, from processing financial data to preparing reports, can now be automated or completed more efficiently with the help of AI.

That might raise an obvious question: if AI can take on more accounting tasks, what does that mean for the people doing the job?

The answer isn't that accounting will stay exactly the same. The way accountants work is already changing as technology becomes more capable and widely used across the profession.

But does that mean accountants will become less important? Or could AI actually change the role in ways that make human expertise more valuable?

In this article, we look at what AI can do in accounting, where human input is still needed and how the skills accountants use are likely to evolve as the technology develops.

## AI can automate accounting tasks, but not the whole job

AI is already capable of handling many repetitive tasks that form part of an accountant's day-to-day work.

But these tasks are only part of an accountant's role. Accountants also need to understand where information has come from, assess whether it can be trusted, interpret what it means for the organisation and use their professional knowledge to decide what action should be taken.

They also need to communicate financial data and complex analysis clearly, adapting how they present information to suit different audiences and help people understand what the findings mean for their decisions.

The table below highlights the difference between the tasks AI supports and the human expertise accountants bring to them:

AI can help with Accountants still provide

Processing large amounts of financial data Professional judgement

Classifying transactions Understanding of business context

Invoice processing Identifying potential discrepancies

Bank reconciliations Interpretation of financial information

Identifying patterns and anomalies Applying accounting knowledge to make decisions

Drafting reports and summaries Communicating findings and recommendations appropriate to each stakeholder

Supporting forecasts and analysis Challenging and interpreting information and assessing risk

As routine processes become more automated, accountants are likely to spend less time on repetitive tasks and more time applying judgement, analysis and critical thinking to the information AI produces.

## Accountants provide judgement and context

AI can identify changes in financial performance and highlight the relevant data, but it can't necessarily explain what caused those changes or what they mean in the context of a particular business.

For example, an accountant investigating an unexpected change may need to consider:

- The circumstances surrounding a transaction
- The wider financial position of the organisation
- How accounting standards apply to a particular situation
- Potential risks
- Whether the available information is complete and reliable
- What the findings mean for the people making business decisions

These considerations require accountants to apply their knowledge and judgement to the information available, rather than simply identify what has changed.

AI can help by making it quicker to find and analyse relevant information, but accountants still need to assess the situation and determine how that information should be used.

## Trust and accountability still matter

Financial information can influence important decisions. It can affect how a business invests, manages its finances, reports to stakeholders and assesses risk, with implications for investors, regulators, employees and customers. That means accuracy and trust remain crucial, even as AI makes financial processes faster.

AI's output is only as reliable as the information and instructions behind it. Poor-quality data, inappropriate instructions or limitations within an AI system can all lead to inaccurate or misleading results.

This makes human oversight particularly important when the consequences of an error are significant. Accountants can help identify potential issues, verify important information and make sure AI is being used appropriately within the organisation.

Ultimately, organisations need clear accountability for how AI-generated information is checked, interpreted and used. This includes making sure there is appropriate oversight when AI is used to support financial processes and decision-making.

## The skills accountants need may change

As AI takes on more routine processes, the skills accountants use in their roles may evolve. Technical accounting knowledge will remain important, but accountants may also need to become increasingly comfortable working with technology, critically evaluating AI-generated information and understanding its limitations.

This will make skills such as these increasingly valuable:

- Data analysis and interpretation
- Digital and AI literacy
- Critical thinking
- Communication
- Problem-solving
- Professional judgement

The exact impact will depend on the type of accounting work involved, the technology an organisation adopts and how effectively it is implemented. But accountants who can combine their technical knowledge with the ability to work effectively alongside AI will be well placed to adapt as the profession changes.

Technology is one of the three core themes of the Next Generation ACA syllabus, alongside sustainability and ethics. This reflects the broader range of knowledge and skills that accountants will need as AI technologies become a bigger part of their work.

ACCA is also placing greater emphasis on data and technology, with changes coming as part of the Accountancy Redefined Syllabus Update. It’s performance management subjects will evolve to further reflect the growing importance of data analytics and performance insights.

Its Strategic Data Science option, will also provide an opportunity to explore data science in greater depth. These developments reflect the broader range of knowledge and skills that accountants may need as technology becomes a bigger part of their work. Together, these developments highlight the importance of combining accounting expertise with digital and analytical skills.

For learners preparing for a career in accounting, developing this combination of technical and digital skills can help them prepare for the changing demands of the profession.

Finance professionals can develop their data analysis skills through programmes that combine financial knowledge with practical data skills. For example, Kaplan’s Level 3 Finance Analyst apprenticeship brings together finance and data, helping learners develop skills to analyse information and support business decision-making.

For those looking to build more specialised data skills, Kaplan’s Analytics in Power BI: ICAEW Certificate covers analysing data, building reports and dashboards, and using data to inform decisions. Kaplan’s Data and Technology programmes also support the development of digital and AI capabilities

## How can accountants prepare for an AI-powered future?

No one can predict exactly what accounting will look like in five or ten years. There are practical steps you can take now to prepare for change.

### 1. Stay curious about new technology

Exploring new AI and digital tools can help you understand where they can be useful in your work.

Start with tasks you already carry out regularly and consider whether AI could make any part of the process more efficient. Following developments in the profession and learning from how your organisation uses new technology can also help you build familiarity without trying to change everything at once.

### 2. Understand how AI is being used

Different organisations will use AI in different ways, so understanding how it is being applied in your workplace can help you use it appropriately. Pay attention to which processes are being automated, how outputs are checked and where human input is still required.

It's also important to understand any policies your organisation has around using AI. This includes what information can be entered into AI tools, which systems are approved for use and when outputs need to be reviewed before they are used. Knowing these boundaries will help you use AI responsibly as well as effectively.

### 3. Look for opportunities to apply your skills differently

As technology takes care of more routine processes, there may be opportunities to take on work that involves greater analysis, collaboration or problem-solving. Think about where your existing accounting knowledge can be applied beyond the tasks you carry out today.

### 4. Keep your skills up to date

The technology used in accounting will continue to develop, so professional development is likely to remain important. This could involve taking a formal qualification, completing shorter courses on new technologies or learning from colleagues who are already using AI in their work.

The most useful approach will depend on your role and the technology being introduced, but regular learning will help you keep pace with changes as they happen.

### 5. Be prepared to adapt

There won't be one fixed version of the AI-powered accountant. The technology, processes and skills required will continue to change, and different accounting roles will be affected in different ways. Being willing to learn and adapt can help you respond to those changes as they happen.

## So, is accounting still a good career?

Yes. AI will change the way accountants work, but it won't remove the need for professional judgement and people who can understand the wider context behind financial information.

The profession will continue to evolve, and accountants will need to keep developing their skills alongside technology. So for anyone willing to adapt and continue learning, we believe accounting will still offer a rewarding and varied career.

Explore Kaplan's professional accounting qualifications and find the right course for your career goals.

## FAQs

### Will AI replace accountants?

AI is unlikely to remove the need for accountants altogether. While some routine tasks can be automated, accountants are still needed to apply professional judgement, understand business context and assess how financial information should be used.

### What should accountants consider before using AI at work?

Accountants should understand how their organisation expects AI to be used, including which tools are approved, what information can be entered into them and when outputs need to be checked. Following these guidelines can help ensure AI is used appropriately and responsibly.

### Can AI improve accountants' productivity?

AI can help accountants work more efficiently by reducing the time spent on some routine processes and making it quicker to find, process and analyse financial information. The time saved could allow accountants to focus on work that requires greater analysis, judgement and collaboration.

### What are the risks of using AI in accounting?

AI can produce inaccurate or misleading information if it is based on poor-quality data, inappropriate instructions or limitations within the system. Accountants therefore need to understand the information AI produces and check important outputs before they are used.

### What opportunities could AI create for accountants?

As AI takes on more routine processes, accountants may have more opportunities to focus on areas such as analysis, problem-solving, communication and business decision-making. The opportunities will vary depending on the role and how AI is adopted by an organisation.

title: Russia “ever-present danger” after Litvinenko murder warns KC | ULaw
text:
24 Nov 2026

Ben Emmerson KC, a leading human rights barrister who acted for the Litvinenko family, brands Vladimir Putin a “common criminal dressed up as a head of state”.

He describes Russian state-sponsored assassinations as a form of “asymmetrical warfare” against the West designed to de-stabilise their institutions.

On the continuing threat from Russia: “It’s an ever-present danger in every respect.”

On Putin, he says - recalling his opening speech at the public inquiry into Litvinenko’s death: “Putin is no more than a common criminal dressed up as a head of state.”

On Russian state-sponsored assassinations: “It’s a form of asymmetrical warfare designed to destabilise the state and its institutions.”

### NEW PODCAST SERIES: Inside the Case

Eighth episode: "The Poisoning of Alexander Litvinenko"

Alexander Litvinenko died on November 23, 2006, in London, aged 43, after being poisoned with radioactive polonium-210.

Twenty years on, the barrister who represented his widow warns that Russia remains an “ever-present danger” to the West.

Ben Emmerson KC, who achieved the setting up of the public inquiry into Litvinenko’s murder, repeats his denunciation at that inquiry of Vladimir Putin as “no more than a common criminal dressed up as a head of state”.

He warns that Russian state-sponsored assassinations form part of a wider strategy to destabilise Western nations and undermine their institutions.

His comments come in the latest episode of The University of Law’s video podcast, Inside the Case, where he also criticises the West for its inconsistent stance towards Putin and warns of the dangers of undermining international law.

His warnings come ahead of the 20th anniversary of Litvinenko’s death on November 23 and coincides with the publication of his widow Marina’s new memoir, A Life in Fragments: Our Love, His Murder, My Resistance, published by Bloomsbury on 5 November 2026.

In it she talks of her struggle to secure justice and her aim for her husband’s murder to be seen as part of a wider pattern of attacks of opponents, extending beyond Russia’s borders.

The 2016 public inquiry in London concluded that her husband was murdered by Andrei Lugovoy and Dmitry Kovtun, probably acting under the direction of the FSB - and that Putin probably approved the operation.

In 2021 the European Court of Human Rights held Russia responsible for Litvinenko’s death and ordered it to pay Marina 100,000 Euros in damages - which has never been paid. The men identified as responsible have not faced any criminal trial. One has since died.

Emmerson describes the battle Marina Litvenenko faced in securing a public inquiry - where she was at risk of legal costs that would mean she would lose her home.

Theresa May, then Prime Minister, had refused the public inquiry. “She [Marina] was treated like a nuisance litigant at this point, and the government not only refused to conduct the inquiry, but they refused to agree a costs arrangement that would enable her to go into this without fear of having to pay a huge government bill.”

The risk of costs “was being held against her over her head like a Sword of Damocles” and “being done deliberately to discourage her from going on with it.”

But, he says, she was determined to go ahead. “Marina is an extraordinary woman. She was determined, obviously, but dignified and courageous every step of the way.

“She told me at one point she couldn’t really move on with her life until she had, if you like, done justice to the man whom she loved, the love of her life, namely to pursue that question…. on whose orders was he killed? The very question that he himself had posed in his dying days.”

The decision to assassinate Litvinenko, Emmerson says, was taken at the “very top of the state of the Russian Federation - and “fundamentally, it was a murder - albeit it was deeply embedded in international politics - it was “a murder of a man for his beliefs.”

There was evidence, he adds, of Putin’s close relationship with one of the murderers: when evidence of his guilt became conclusive, Putin “called him in and pinned a medal for services to the motherland onto his chest.”

On the opening day of the inquiry, when Emmerson had made his speech about Putin being a criminal dressed up as a head of state, within hours Russian fighter jets buzzed the coast of Cornwall, entering British airspace and then leaving.

It was an unprecedented case, he recalls. “It was a carefully planned operation which had involved two or three visits to London. And once the isotope had been identified, it was possible for the police to trace the movements of these two individuals as though they were Hansel and Gretel leaving a trail behind them.”

In the end, the proof turned on a collection of debris in the u-bend of a wash basin in a hotel bedroom because security cameras could prove there was only one person inside that room at that time. After the poisoning, the excess polonium had been poured down the sink and collected among the debris in the u-bend.

“It’s often said that there’s one piece of evidence in a case that really everything turns on. It can often be something very apparently insignificant. And in a way, the dirt and the filth that went into this murder found its expression in the fact that the final key to proving their guilt was the dirty debris in the u-bend of a public [wash basin].”

The case was a “life-changing experience for me”, he says, “where the stakes were as high as they could possibly be, with the client who earned my admiration and respect within the first meeting that we had. She’s the epitome of a person with dignity and courage.”

## Course Overview

Are you excited about helping people thrive at work, but want a supportive first step before diving into a full honours degree? Our BA (Hons) Business Management (Human Resource Management) with Foundation Year gives you the essential academic study skills you need to succeed at university, followed by specialist HR and people management skills for today's workplaces.

The BA (Hons) Business Management (Human Resource Management) degree combines a broad understanding of business with specialist knowledge of employee engagement, digital people management, workforce analytics and organisational change.

Arden's foundation year modules have been designed to give you a tailored and fully supportive introduction to university study. ## Patricia Ovuoke Oseh content

### About me

- Social Impact Practitioner & Public Speaker
- Studied: BA (Hons) Financial Studies, 2016 and PG Cert Business Administration, 2023

### About my career

I chose to study in the UK for its reputation for academic excellence and professional development. Manchester Met appealed to me because of its strong reputation, diverse student community and welcoming environment. Studying in a multicultural city offered an opportunity to learn from people of different backgrounds and broaden my perspective.

After graduating, I channelled my knowledge and experience into social impact work, founding the Moral Values and Ethics Support Foundation (MoVES Foundation). Through this work, as a Social Impact Practitioner and Public Speaker, I have developed initiatives supporting women and girls, young people and communities, alongside public speaking and advocacy focused on moral values, ethics and positive social change.

Through MoVES Foundation, I develop and coordinate programmes, deliver talks, mentor young people, advocate for responsible citizenship and build partnerships to address social challenges. My work spans on-the-ground initiatives in Africa and online engagement, enabling me to reach diverse audiences, share knowledge and inspire positive change across communities. I am passionate about character development, ethical leadership and empowering individuals to recognise their potential and contribute meaningfully to society.

My degree helped me develop analytical thinking, financial literacy, research, problem-solving, planning and organisational skills. These have been particularly valuable in my social impact work, where I develop initiatives, manage resources, coordinate programmes, build partnerships and make strategic decisions. My academic background has provided a strong foundation for translating ideas into practical projects, managing competing priorities and working towards sustainable outcomes. The combination of financial knowledge and business understanding continues to support my leadership, programme development and commitment to creating positive social change.

Since graduating, I have completed a PGCert in Business Administration at Manchester Met and undertaken further professional training including a Diploma in Mental Health . I developed the Girl Child Leadership Training Programme, impacting over 20,000 girls in Nigeria and online. My public speaking, safeguarding and research training continue to strengthen my leadership and social impact work.

### My top tip for students

Be intentional, stay curious and never underestimate the power of networking. Identify your strengths, keep developing relevant skills, seek opportunities to gain practical experience and build genuine professional relationships. Do not be afraid to start small or explore unconventional paths. Your degree opens doors, but your initiative and resilience can help you achieve even more.

### I’m inspired by

The opportunity to empower others, especially women, girls and young people, to discover their potential, develop their character and become positive influences in their communities. Seeing how purposeful action can transform lives motivates me to keep learning, creating opportunities and contributing to meaningful social change.

### Why I love Manchester Met

I appreciated the diverse, multicultural environment, the opportunity to learn from people of different backgrounds, and the support, approachability and dedication of the university staff.

# Get ready for Manchester Met

Everything you need to know after receiving your offer from Manchester Met.

## Course search bar

### Find out more about your course

## Congratulations on your offer

Congratulations on receiving an offer from Manchester Met.

An exciting new chapter awaits you at the Modern University of the Year 2026 and 2027, with a Gold-rated student experience and a campus at the heart of one of the UK’s top student cities.

Here you will find support that will help you get ready for university, with guidance on accommodation, careers and employability opportunities, ways to connect with other students, and support to prepare for life at Manchester Met.

Need to get in touch with us? If you have further questions, we’re here to help.

## You've received your offer, what next?

This step-by-step guide will walk you through everything you need to do before September, from accepting your offer and arranging your finances to preparing for your first week.

Understand your offer

### Understand your offer

Now you have received your offer, take a few minutes to read the important information about your course, admissions policies, student contract, and terms and conditions.

Read more about your offer.

#### Conditional offer

A conditional offer means you need to meet specific requirements before your place can be confirmed, such as achieving certain exam results.

Your offer may be based on:

- Specific grades (e.g. ABB at A level or DDM in a BTEC Extended Diploma)
- A ‘tariff’ offer (e.g. 128 UCAS tariff points from A levels)
- It might also ask for a minimum grade in a specific level three subject, to ensure that you have the necessary knowledge and skills for your chosen course. (e.g. 128 tariff points plus a grade C in A level Maths)

Please note: Manchester Met does not accept tariff points from AS level qualifications.

Once you’ve met the conditions, we’ll update your offer to unconditional in your UCAS Hub and send enrolment details. For most students, this usually happens in August on A level results day.

You’ll find the full details of your offer in your UCAS Hub.

Aspirational offer

If your offer is higher than your current predicted grades, we may have made you an aspirational offer. Aspirational offers reflect our belief in your potential to achieve strong results.

If you accept your offer and then do not achieve the exact grades required, we will still review your application ahead of A-level results day (Thursday 12 August 2027). Every applicant is considered individually, and we may still be able to confirm your place.

#### Unconditional offer

An unconditional offer means you’ve already met the entry requirements.

You may still need to:

- Provide evidence of your qualifications.
- Complete additional checks, such as a DBS check.

We’ll contact you with further enrolment information, usually in August.

Accept your offer

### Accept your offer

Once you have received decisions from all your university choices, you will be able to select a firm and an insurance choice on your UCAS hub.

UCAS will give you a deadline to respond to your offers, but you can respond before this if you are comfortable that you have the information you need to make your decision.

If you have any questions you’d like to ask before deciding on your choices, don’t hesitate to get in touch.

If you’re ready to accept your offer, log in to your UCAS hub.

Book a visit day

### Book a visit day

Applicant visit days are exclusively for Manchester Met offer holders and give you the chance to experience your course before you start university.

The majority of our courses have a visit day, and after you’ve received your offer, you’ll receive your visit day invite. Even if you’ve already visited us at an open day, we highly recommend attending a visit day as it offers you an opportunity to spend a day experiencing life as a student on your course.

If you have any questions about visit days please email us with your full name and MMU ID (or UCAS ID) at [email protected].

Find your home in our student accommodation

### Find your home in our student accommodation

Living in student accommodation is a great way to meet new people, settle into university life and feel part of the community from day one.

With Manchester Met accommodation, your rent is all-inclusive and covers high-speed internet and wi-fi, utilities and contents insurance and staff available 24/7.

Once you have made Manchester Met your firm choice, you can take the first step in booking your student accommodation. Typically, bookings open in March.

Full time, first-year undergraduate students, including foundation year students, are guaranteed a room with us or one of our approved accommodation partners if you complete your booking and pay the rental pre-payment by Monday 31 August 2027.

Take a look at your accommodation options now and find out how to book.

Apply for student finance

### Apply for student finance

To make sure your funding is ready for the start of term, it’s important to apply for student finance as early as possible.

To apply for a tuition fee or maintenance loan, Student Finance England applications usually open between February and March.
